title: Life Hacking for Educators
text:
Overview
Life hacks help us streamline our lives and make us feel clever—a not insignificant source of joy in these difficult times. As educators, many of us are invigorated by the positive energy we get from our students, and enervated by the drudgery of administrative tasks, often made more manual and more painful by opaque software systems. In this session, we celebrate our most clever and useful tricks for minimizing the headaches we incur from learning management systems and other academic edifices (e.g., Moodle, Canvas, Workday, etc.)
Session chair: Andrew Bray - Berkeley
Session organizer: Ben Baumer - Smith College

title: The LTS Document: Lab, Template and Solutions All in One
text: Assigning low-stakes practice problems or “lab” activities during class is one strategy for incorporating active learning into a traditional lecture-oriented course. In a course that incorporates computation, instructors may find it useful to provide a document with detailed information and instructions (a “lab” document), a document with initial scaffolding for students to work within (a “template” document), and a document with example results (a “solutions” document). However, keeping content synchronized across these three documents, as well as the learning management system used to distribute these documents, introduces administrative overhead and mistakes. This talk demonstrates how to use an LTS document (a custom document format for the Quarto publishing system) to create each of these student-facing files simultaneously from one main instructor-facing file, and automatically deploy them to Moodle using an R package.

title: Stop Repeating Yourself
section: Rapid Overview of an R Package
text:
Rapid Overview of an R Package

An R package is just a folder with a specific structure
Two ingredients: code + documentation
R/RStudio tools (like devtools) know how to read that structure


mypackage/
├── DESCRIPTION          <- metadata: name, version, author, dependencies
├── NAMESPACE            <- what functions are exported to users
├── R/
│   ├── clean_data.R     <- your functions live here
│   └── plot_helper.R
├── man/
│   ├── clean_data.Rd    <- help files (auto-generated!)
│   └── plot_helper.Rd
├── data/
│   └── class_survey.rda <- optional: built-in datasets
└── vignettes/
    └── intro.Rmd        <- optional: long-form tutorials


If you can organize files into folders and comment your code, you can build a package


Learn more: https://r-pkgs.org

title: Stop Repeating Yourself

Generating alt text

Prompt:
Please create alt text for this set of box plots for the number of seconds songs in the top 100 of the billboard charts last (duration).


Result:
This image features a series of vertical box-and-whisker plots titled “Length of #1 hits by decade,” illustrating the duration of top-charting songs in seconds from the 1950s through the 2020s.
The chart shows a clear historical trend where the median song length gradually increased from approximately 150 seconds in the 1950s to a peak of about 250 seconds in the 1990s, followed by a steady decline back toward 200 seconds in the 2020s. The 1970s and 1980s exhibit significant upward outliers, with some tracks reaching between 400 and 500 seconds, while the 2020s include an extreme outlier extending above 600 seconds. Overall, the 1950s have the most compact distribution with the shortest durations, while the 1990s show the highest consistent song lengths with the fewest outliers.

title: Stop Repeating Yourself
text:
Rapid Overview of Quarto Live

Quarto Live is an extension that lets you embed live, runnable R (or Python) code cells directly into a Quarto reveal.js slide or webpage
Powered by WebR — R runs entirely in the student’s browser, no server or install required
Students can edit code and see results instantly, right on the slide or page


The only syntax change: swap the chunk engine


Regular R chunk:
```{r}
lm(rating ~ complaints, data = attitude)
```



Quarto Live R chunk:
```{webr}
lm(rating ~ complaints, data = attitude)
```




If you can write a normal Quarto code chunk, you can make it interactive — just change r to webr.

Speaker

Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel is a Professor of the Practice and Associate Director of Undergraduate Studies in the Department of Statistical Science as well as the Director of First-Year Experience in Trinity College of Arts & Sciences at Duke University. She is also Senior Developer Advocate at Posit. Mine is a leading voice in modern statistics and data science education. Her work focuses on integrating reproducible computing, open-source tools, and real-world data into the statistics curriculum, transforming how students engage with data and statistical thinking. She is a co-author of R for Data Science, the creator and maintainer of Data Science in a Box, and she teaches popular data analysis and data science with R courses on Coursera.. She is also a core contributor to the OpenIntro project and an advocate for open educational resources and statistical computing in R. A Fellow of the American Statistical Association and an Elected Member of the International Statistical Institute, she has received numerous honors, including the ASA’s Waller Education Award and the Robert V. Hogg Award for Excellence in Teaching Introductory Statistics. She currently serves as Vice President of the International Association for Statistical Education (IASE) and as co-chair of the ASA’s DataFest Steering Committee. Through her teaching, writing, and advocacy, Dr. ÇetinkayaRundel has advanced accessible, computation-rich, and reproducible data science education worldwide.

title: Automate all the things
text: Teaching modern data science and statistics courses presents numerous logistical challenges—from building and distributing assignments and other course materials to providing timely, consistent feedback. In this talk, we explore tools for automating the repetitive aspects of course administration, building on the core reproducible infrastructure of Git, GitHub, and Quarto. Examples will include the ghclass package, which streamlines classroom management on GitHub, enabling automated repository creation, assignment distribution, and collection. GitHub Actions, which extends this ecosystem with CI pipelines that automatically render documents, run checks, and provide feedback on student submissions. The q2r and markermd packages, which offer programmatic tools for parsing and manipulating Quarto and R Markdown documents, enabling both automated and more efficient manual assessment of student work. Finally, we look ahead to the emerging role of agentic AI tools in teaching, discussing both the opportunities and considerations for AI-driven automation in course management.

title: Stop Repeating Yourself: Shared R Resources to Reduce Duplicated Prep
text: For introductory statistics courses that incorporate programming, a lot of time is spent creating and maintaining how-to guides and design class activities that introduce help students get up and running with the language, navigating the IDE, fundamental building blocks of the programming language, and practicing the commands to carryout analyses. This takes a lot of time and effort, which can be duplicated across faculty when there are many sections of the same course taught in a term. In this talk, we explore the use of an R “lab manual” paired with an R package that serves as a shared resource for the introductory statistics courses at Carleton College. We’ll discuss its usage, maintenance, and frustration-saving features. Along the way we’ll also discus a smattering of other “life hacks”, such as generating alternative text with AI and using quarto-live for class activities.

title: gglm: A tool for teaching linear model diagnostics while adhering to the grammar of graphics
text: In this talk, I’ll discuss the gglm R package, which allows for easy creation of linear model diagnostic plots using the grammar of the graphics and ggplot2. More specifically, gglm provides a consistent and intuitive syntax to produce residual diagnostic plots for a variety of model types. We’ll cover the basics of the package, along with motivation and use cases for a modern statistics, statistical learning, or data science classroom. We’ll compare gglm’s diagnostic plot solution to solutions provided by base R and others. We’ll then discuss features of the package that allow for more robust analysis of residuals than typical model diagnostic tools, including different model types (i.e., engines) and multivariate diagnostics. Finally, I’ll showcase a shiny dashboard that allows the user to upload data, build a statistical model, and produce diagnostics powered by gglm, aimed at introductory statistics courses that don’t cover programming, but still want to use real data.

title: "Lab 1: Getting Acquainted with R, RStudio and Quarto"
editor: source
format: lts-html:
---

## Creating Objects

You can think of *objects* as boxes that store things. To create an object, we have to ask R to take the results of some code and *assign* those results to an object. We can do this using the **assignment operator** `<-`, which is often called the arrow. In your code, you write the assignment operator iby typing in the "less than" symbol, followed by a dash.

::: question
In the console, type in `result <- 5 + 2` and press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to run the code.

Then, type in `applesauce <- 10 * 3` in the console and press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to run the code.

Then, write an answer the following questions in your Lab 1 Quarto document:

- What happens in the RStudio "Environment" pane when you use the assignment operator to create a new object?
- What *doesn't* happen in the console when you use the assignment operator to create a new object?
:::

::: solution
- The name of each object is shown, along with its computed value.
- The computed result is *not* printed out
:::

::: question
In your template file, locate the code chunk that looks like this:

```{r}
#| echo: fenced
result <- 5 + 2
applesauce <- 10 * 3
```

Enter a blank line at the end of this code chunk, and write the command `result + applesauce` on the blank line. Then click the green triangle "play" button in the upper right hand corner of the code chunk to execute the code in the chunk. What is the result?
:::

::: solution
```{r}
result + applesauce
```

The output is 37 - the same value you would get if you ran `5 + 2` + `10 * 3` in the console!
:::

title: The LTS Document
text:
How Does it Work?

Each lts-html document is parsed using a Quarto project pre-rendering script (written in Lua for portability)

The .question divs are written into a new *_template.qmd file
The .solution divs are written into a new *_solutions.qmd file

The lab, template, and solutions are rendered into HTML documents

A pandoc filter strips all .solution divs from the main lab file during rendering

title: The LTS Document
text:
Getting Started with LTS
To start a new project:
quarto use template wjhopper/lts


Within an existing project:
quarto add wjhopper/lts


Then manually add the pre-render script to the project’s _quarto.yml configuration file, e.g.,
project:
  type: website
  pre-render: _extensions/wjhopper/lts/setup.lua

text:
MoodleR Spotlight: Creating and Populating Groups
Normally, creating 5 new groups and populating them with 3 members each would require manual data entry for group and person, and several dozens of clicks


But with moodleR, it’s two lines of code =)

moodleR::create_groups(
  tab,
  groups = unique(groups$group_name)
  )
moodleR::populate_groups(tab, groups)

title: The LTS Document
text:
MoodleR Spotlight: Project Rotation Schedules
In SDS 100, we have a phased group project where students collaborate on an exploratory data analysis


Each student chooses their own data set, and starts their own report

Each week, they rotate data sets, and pick up the report where their group mate left off


We help students keep track of who’s doing what each week by posting a project rotation schedule
